title: The Weight of Scientific Trust
text:
Scientists who publish research occupy a position of considerable trust, because the public rarely has the expertise to verify their claims. This trust carries an obligation to report findings honestly, including results that are inconvenient or unexpected. Yet the pressure to produce striking headlines can tempt researchers to overstate modest conclusions. Such exaggeration, however well intentioned, can mislead both policymakers and ordinary readers.

Many universities have therefore introduced formal codes of conduct that address data fabrication and selective reporting. Critics argue that these codes are often vague and rarely enforced. Nevertheless, supporters maintain that written standards at least establish a shared vocabulary for discussing misconduct. Ultimately, the credibility of science depends less on rules than on the personal integrity of each researcher.

questions.text: According to paragraph one, why is the public's trust in scientists significant?
options: They always publish results that are later confirmed.
The public rarely has the expertise to verify their claims.
They are required to produce striking headlines.

questions.text: According to paragraph two, what do critics say about the codes of conduct?
options: They are too detailed to be understood.
They are often vague and rarely enforced.
They have been removed by all universities.

questions.text: What is the author's main point in the final sentence of the passage?
options: Strict rules matter more than personal character.
Journalists should replace scientists as public experts.
Scientific credibility rests mainly on each researcher's integrity.
Codes of conduct should be abolished.

questions.text: Why does the author describe exaggeration as 'however well intentioned'?
options: To suggest that exaggeration is always deliberate.
To show that misleading claims can come from good motives.
To argue that headlines should be banned.
To claim that researchers never exaggerate.

vocabulary.definition: specialised knowledge or skill in a particular field
the act of presenting something as larger or better than it really is
the quality of being trusted and believed
the quality of being honest and having strong moral principles

paragraph_translations: Cientistas que publicam pesquisas ocupam uma posição de grande confiança, porque o público raramente tem o conhecimento necessário para verificar suas afirmações. Essa confiança traz a obrigação de relatar os resultados com honestidade, inclusive os que são inconvenientes ou inesperados. No entanto, a pressão por manchetes impressionantes pode levar pesquisadores a exagerar conclusões modestas. Tal exagero, por mais bem-intencionado que seja, pode induzir em erro tanto formuladores de políticas quanto leitores comuns.

Muitas universidades, portanto, introduziram códigos de conduta formais que tratam da fabricação de dados e da seleção de resultados. Críticos argumentam que esses códigos costumam ser vagos e raramente são aplicados. Ainda assim, os defensores sustentam que normas escritas ao menos estabelecem um vocabulário comum para discutir a má conduta. Em última análise, a credibilidade da ciência depende menos de regras do que da integridade pessoal de cada pesquisador.
